source_refs.note: Half-Wave Rectifier: a main subheading of 17.14 Rectification, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 106-107.

blocks.text: In a half-wave rectification, an AC signal is converted into pulsating direct current DC by passing one half-cycle of waveform and blocking the other half. In Fig.17.13, alternating voltage of period T called input voltage is supplied to a diode D which is connected in series with a load resistance R_L. The working of half-wave rectifier is based on the fact that the diode allows the current flow only in one direction. Thus, it converts the AC signal into DC signal. Figure 17.13 shows the circuit of half-wave rectification and it is working showing graphically its input and output wave forms.

blocks.alt: Top: a transformer feeds a diode D (forward resistance rf) in series with a load resistor RL; current I, the load current Idc and the output voltage Vdc are marked. Bottom left: the AC voltage input signal against time, 0, 90 and 180 degrees marked. Bottom right: the DC voltage output signal; the positive half-cycles are passed (conducting) and the output is zero during the negative half-cycles (cut off).
blocks.caption: Figure 17.13: Working of a half-wave rectifier, showing graphically its input and output wave forms (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.13).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed output graph of Figure 17.13 still shows the negative half-cycles. The diode blocks them, so the output is zero there, as drawn above.

During positive half-cycle of the input alternating voltage i.e., during the interval 0→T/2, the diode D is forward bias, so it offers a very low resistance and current flows through R_L. The flow of current through R_L causes a potential drop across it which varies in accordance with the alternating input (Fig.17.13).

blocks.text: A circuit board view of half-wave rectifier with its different components

blocks.alt: Block diagram: 220 V AC goes to a rectifier, then to a battery, then to an inverter and on to the AC appliance. Below the rectifier a battery charger takes its output and feeds the battery. A note reads: rectifiers are used in UPS at homes for backup power.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.13 (a): A circuit view of a UPS system used in our homes (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.13 (a)).

blocks.text: During negative half cycle, during the interval T/2→T, the diode becomes reverse bias and offers a very high résistance, so practically no current flows through R_L and potential drop across it is almost zero (Fig.17.13). The same events repeat during the next cycle and so on. The current across R_L flows in only one direction which means it is direct current. However, this current flows in pulses. The voltage which appears across load resistance R_L is known as output voltage.
